div.p: The reliability of the design of a real-time system is important. For example, when there are errors in avionics control systems or nuclear reactor control systems, the loss ofJnance, time or even the loss of human lives could be enormous. Therefore when one designs a real-time system, methods to guarantee the correctness of the system are needed before the implementation of the system. We specih a scheduling algorithm ojreal-time systems called Priori0 Ceiling Protocol using ACSR-VPandpe@orm schedulability analysis on real-time systems by checking for a bisimulation relation.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: To improve reliability of real-time systems, there must be correct specification and complete verification of the systems in the design phase. In this paper we use formal methods to design real-time systems and by doing this we can improve the reliability of real-time systems. Formal methods have been used to design and verify hardwares andlor software systems. Because they are based on mathematics and logics, we can describe a system without ambiguity and prove the equivalence between the implementation of the system and requirements of the system by the mathematical property of formal methods. We can reduce the potential disaster and loss of time associated with an incorrect operation of real-time systems by checking the correctness of the systems before the implementation using formal methods.
One of the formal methods that can be used in modeling real-time systems is ACSR (Algebra of Communicating Shared Resources) [3].

ACSR is based on CCS(Ca1culus for Communicating Systems)[ I ] and includes the concepts of time, resource, priority that are needed in concurrency theory. ACSR can *This research was supported in part by IITA 96024-IT1-11. be used in specifying and verifying real-time systems. By using ACSR we can describe a system in which many processes use shared resources and model a situation of concurrent executions of many processes and communications among processes. The dynamic priority and value-passing communication are needed to the better schedulability analysis of real-time systems scheduled by priority. For this purpose, ACSR-VP(A1gebra of Communicating Shared Resources with Value Passing) [2,4] was developed to support dynamic priority and value-passing communication. Therefore, in this paper we use ACSR-VP in specifying and verifying a real-time system scheduled by a scheduling algorithm called Priority Ceiling Protocol(PCP). To verify real-time systems specified by ACSR-VP, we check whether the systems is schedulable.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the syntax and semantics of ACSR-VP. Section 3 introduces the verification method for real-time systems specified by ACSR-VP. ACSR-VP specification and verification of a real-time system scheduled by PCP are represented in section 4. The paper is concluded with section 5.

div.head: ACSR-VP(A1gebra of Communicating Shared Resources with Value Passing)
div.p: This section presents the syntax and operational semantics of ACSR-VP[2], which is an extension of ACSR. ACSR is a timed process algebra based on the synchronization model of CCS that includes features for representing synchronization, time, temporal scopes [9], resource requirements, and priorities. Although the time domain of ACSR can be either discrete [3] or dense [8], this paper uses discrete time exclusively since the systems we are modeling are typically scheduled using clocks with discrete granularities. Primitive actions consists of two kinds of actions: timed actions and instantaneous events. A timed action A E V R takes one time unit to execute and is represented as a list of resources. A distinguished timed action { } > or 0, stands for 0-8186-8073-3197 $10.00 0 1997 IEEE one time unit of idling. An instantaneous event e takes no time to execute and is represented as a pair of a label and its priority, e.g., (chan, 3). A distinguished event label T is used to represent the synchronization of events.

ACSR-VP extends the discrete time version of ACSR [3] with dynamic priorities and value-passing mechanism as follows: 1) priorities can be value expressions containing variables, e.g., { ( C P U , y + 1)) is a timed action; 2 ) instantaneous events are augmented with a value expression to represent value-passing. For example, (I?x, 3) is an input event that receives a value in 2, and (I!5, y) is an output event that sends 5; 3) processes can have parameters. For example, a process constant Job with two parameters can be invoked by executing Job(O,5), feeding 0 and 5 as the actual parameters.

We use 2 , y for value variables, we, we] for value expressions and be, bel for boolean expressions. We denote a vector of value variables and value expressions as z and vie, respectively. Also, we use I , 21 to denote event labels and r , r1 to denote resources. F and I represent sets of event labels and resources, respectively. Furthermore, we use C to stand for a process constant. +

div.head: Schedulability Analysis of Real-Time Systems in ACSR-VP
div.p: To verify the correctness of the real-time systems specified by ACSR-VP, we perform schedulability analysis. Schedulability analysis checks whether or not a real-time system scheduled by a particular scheduling algorithm misses any of its deadlines. And when a system can finish its jobs in a given deadline, we say that the system is schedulable. Therefore we can verify that a specification of a real-time system is correct by showing that the system specified by ACSR-VP is schedulable. In this section we introduce schedulability analysis of real-time systems based on equivalence check between ACSR-VP processes.

To facilitate the analysis of ACSR specification we have used the Verification, Execution, and Rewriting System for ACSR (VERSA)[S, 61. VERSA is an interactive toolkit that includes features for algebrac analysis, equivalence checking, state-space analysis and interactive execution of ACSR process expressions. The correctness of the realtime system presented in this paper has been verified with the assistance of the VERSA system.

For the schedulability analysis of a real-time system specified by ACSR-VP, we construct the correctness specification of the system. The correctness specification means a specification that describes a system more precisely and easy

In correctness specification, all processes proceed in sequence and there are no processes executing in parallel and it is relatively easy to describe a system because it has no value-passing between processes. In contrast to the correctness specification, the implementation specification means a specification in which many processes execute in parallel and communicate each other by value-passing. First, we show that the system specified by the correctness specification is schedulable. Then we show that the implementation specification is equivalent to the correctness specification. By doing this we can verify that the implementation specification is correct. Equivalence relation is introduced below by which the equivalence between ACSR-VP processes can be checked.

div.head: Equivalence Relations
div.p: Equivalence between ACSR processes is based on the concept of bisimulation [ lo], which compares the computation trees of two processes. For a given transition system "-", any binary relation r is a (strong) bisimulation if, for ( P , Q) E r and CY E D , P (or Q) can take a step on a , then Q (or P ) must also be able to take a step on (Y with both of the next states also bisimilar. Weak bisimulation, M ~, is an equivalence relation (though not a congruence) for ACSR that compares observable behaviors of processes.
Bisimulation and weak bisimulation can be checked by welldeveloped algorithms (see [I21 or [13] for a review). These algorithms are guaranteed to terminate on finite labeled transition systems.
In the rest of this paper, we will apply these bisimulations to analyze the specifications of real-time systems which have finite labeled transition systems.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: To verify whether a certain real-time system modeled by ACSR-VP is correct, we need to check whether the system is schedulable. And when a system is schedulable, we can consider that no deadline of the system is missed. If no deadline is missed in a periodic system, the behavior of the system is not finite but infinite by doing same action repeatedly. When we hide all the resources of a system and ignore the internal action, any infinitely repeating ACSR-VP processes in the system is identical to the infinitely repeating idling action 0". Eventually, to guarantee whether a realtime system specified by ACSR-VP is schedulable, we need to check it is weakly bisimilar to 8" with resource-hiding.

We have used VERSA for the checking of the bisimulation between ACSR-VP processes. Note that the infinite idling action means that no job in the system can missed its deadline at any time, that is, it is schedulable. Then, we can verify whether the implementation specification of the real-time system is correct by checking the weak bisimulation between the implementation specification and the correctness specification. div.head: Specification and Verification of Priority Ceiling Protocol Using ACSR-VP
div.p: In real-time systems scheduled by priority-driven preemptive scheduling, priority inversion where a higher priority job must wait for the processing of a lower priority job can happen. To prevent the priority inversion problem, Priority Inheritance Protocol was introduced [7]. But Priority Inheritance Protocol has the problem that it does not prevent deadlocks.

To prevent deadlocks, Priority Ceiling Protocol was introduced [7]. The basic idea of this protocol is the concept of priority ceiling to each semaphore, which is the same as the priority of the highest priority job that use the semaphore. And if a job J wants to enter its critical section, its priority must be higher than the highest priority ceiling of all semaphores currently locked by jobs other than job J . Otherwise J will be blocked and cannot enter the critical section.

In PCP the concept of priority inheritance is applied. When a job J h with a higher priority attempts to lock the semaphore which is not the same semaphore locked by a lower priority job J l , if J h is blocked by the priority ceiling of the semaphore locked by J l , then Jl inherits the priority of J h . The job which inherited the priority of a higher priority job resumes its priority when exits a critical section.

Figure 1 shows that when a deadlock is formed, it can be solved by PCP. The priority ceilings of both semaphores SI and S 2 are equal to the priority of job JI. At time t 3 , job J I tries to enter its critical section by locking the semaphore 5 ' 1 . However, J l ' s priority is not higher than the priority ceiling of the semaphore S 2 locked by job J 2 . Hence, job J1

is blocked and cannot enter its critical section. Job J2 now inherits the priority ofjob J1 and resumes execution. As Jl cannot lock the semaphore S 1 but is suspended instead, the deadlock involving J1 and J 2 is prevented.

div.head: Specification of PCP Using ACSR-VP
div.p: In this section, we specify a real-time system scheduled by PCP using ACSR-VP. We assume that the system has two jobs, J , and J 2 , and they execute nested critical sections. P and V semaphore operations are modeled by processes P, V and as there are two semaphores, i.e., SI and S2, we constructed two processes P1 and P2 for each critical sections. The job sequence of critical sections are described below. The process CS, (i = 1,2) models the execution of the jobs within the first critical section and process CS2; (i = 1, 2) models the execution of the jobs within the second critical section. When the accumulated execution time equals fcs, the process Exec checks the priority ceiling via (plport,l) or (p2port,l). If there is no semaphore locked by another job or a job's priority is higher than the transferred priority ceiling, the job can enter its critical section. But if the job's priority is same as or lower than the transferred priority ceiling, the job is blocked and cannot enter its critical section.

When job J2 executing its critical section blocks job J1, J2 inherits the priority of J1 through port chan. As the critical sections are nested, while a Job executes its first critical section it executes its second critical section. When a job finishes all the critical sections, it unlocks the semaphores via port v and executes its non-critical section.
Each semaphore process V1 and V2 sends its priority ceiling via its port. If the semaphore is unlocked at first time, it sends 0, but when it is locked, it sends its priority ceiling.

div.p: The ACSR-VP specification of PCP process PCPSpec is presented in Figure 3. Note that PCPSpec is sequential; it describes the behavior for two tasks under PCP in a functional form. But in Figure 3, only the specification of jobl is described and the part for job2 is omitted, since the structure of specification of job2 is identical to that of job,. PCP-Spec contains 8 parameters, s,, t,, semi, ip,, i=1,2 where s, represents the accumulated computation time of the task i during the current period, and t , represents the elapsed time from the start of the current period. semi represents which job occupies the semaphore i, that is, semi = 0 means no job is in the semaphore i , and semi = j tells that job j is currently in the semaphore. ipi represents the inherited priority at which a job executes its critical section guarded by semaphore i. At any instant, the task i (i=1,2) is in one of the states based on the conditions on s i , t i , semi, ipi. Some of the states are explained below.

div.head: Executing:
div.p: The task i executes its non-critical section before it reaches the start time of the first critical section and its current deadline is not reached(i.e., si < fcsi and t i < di). The task has to compete the resource cpu to execute its non-critical session job.

2. Deadlock: The task i has not completed its computation on CPU by the end of its deadline (i.e., si < ci and ti = di). The PCPSpec process then becomes NIL, implying that the given set of tasks is not schedulable by PCP.

3. Terminating: The task i has completed its computation on CPU but it has not reached the end of its current period (i.e., si = ci and ti < pi). The task has to wait until the end of its period to start again.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The reliability of the design of real-time system is important. When one designs a real-time system, therefore, methods to guarantee the correctness of the system are needed before the implementation of the system. The reliability of real-time system can be increased by means of formal methods. As formal methods are based on mathematics and logics, one can describe a system without ambiguity or incorrectness using formal methods. And it is effective to use formal methods in a point of time and cost because the system can be verified before its implementation.

In this paper, we specified real-time systems using ACSR-VP(A1gebra of Communicating Shared Resources with Value Passing), which is one of formal methods for real-time systems. ACSR-VP supports the concepts that are needed in describing real-time systems like concurrency, time, and priority, hence we can model real-time systems concisely and correctly using ACSR-VP. By using ACSR-VP, we can describe the behaviors of processes of real-time systems in detail and in a abstract form, and we can verify whether the system is schedulable. The verification of system is done by using the schedulability analysis and the equivalence relation.

We specified a real-time system scheduled by the algorithm called Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) using ACSR-VP and we verified that the specification of the system is correct by the schedulability analysis.
